chunks: As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-ʿAbbās ibn Maʿrūf and ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Ṣalt, from Ṣafwān ibn Yaḥyā, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār, from ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd ibn Abī al-Daylam, who said:
I said to Abī ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام about a man who drinks wine, then spat onto my garment from his saliva. He said: “It is nothing.”

So there is no ambiguity in this report, because he only asked him about the saliva of a wine-drinker, and he said to him: “There is no problem with it.” Saliva does not become impure; rather, the impure thing is only the wine.

key_terms.النَّجِسُ: the impure thing; identified specifically in the text as wine
key_terms.الْخَمْرَ: wine; the intoxicant identified here as najis
key_terms.بُصَاقِهِ: his saliva or spittle, the substance asked about in the ruling
key_terms.ثَوْبِي: my garment, the object affected by the saliva
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ بِهِ: there is no problem with it; a formula indicating permissibility or absence of objection
key_terms.لَيْسَ بِشَيْءٍ: it is of no consequence; indicating no ruling of impurity here
key_terms.يَنْجَسُ: becomes impure; referring here to ritual impurity

ai.seo_question: Is the saliva of a person who drinks wine considered najis on clothing?
ai.summary: This report discusses the ruling concerning saliva from a person who drinks wine when it reaches one’s garment. The text clarifies that the saliva itself is not najis, and that the impurity pertains to the wine itself, making this a jurisprudential discussion of ritual purity.
